step.text:
The issue is that `ChatMessage` currently reads `agentSeed` by matching the item's author ID against available agents, but for helper threads the author is the parent agent (like Bubbles) rather than the helper itself (like Copy). Jamel wants the helper's name and mark to be used instead. Since `ThreadItem` already has author information but the mark is a `SubagentMark`, I need to find the cleanest way to surface the helper's identity through the existing codebase structure.

I'm weighing two approaches: either add a helper field directly to `ThreadItem` so `ChatMessage` can render the `SubagentMark` when present, or have `buildThread` accept an optional identity override that applies the helper name and mark to all agent-authored items in that thread. The second option feels cleaner since it's a single configuration point, and only `SubagentRun` would need to pass this override. But there's a subtlety—the helper's thread also contains the person's own messages if they steer via the composer, and those should stay attributed to the person, not the helper. Only agent-authored items like replies, thinking, and tool calls should get the helper identity, while note items stay as crew.

For the implementation, I need to substitute the helper name where `labelOf(event.agentId, event.agentLabel)` is currently used for agent start and end steps, and set a helper seed field on those items so the mark renders. Steps don't show avatars—only reply items do through `ChatMessage`—so the change is really just for replies. There's also a question about whether wrapping the helper name in `MemberName` makes sense, since hovering would show the agent's card but the name says something else, which could be confusing. Keeping it simple might mean not wrapping it in `MemberName` when it's a helper.

Looking at the design rules, agents always render their deterministic generated pet icon, never an avatar. A helper is different and should get its own generated mark. So the approach is to add a `helperSeed` field to `ThreadItem`, and when it's set, `ChatMessage` draws the helper mark instead of the agent icon, with the name rendered plain text rather than wrapped in `MemberName`. Then `buildThread` gets an optional parameter to specify the identity the agent's words should read under in that thread.

Now I need to check all the call sites for `buildThread` to see how adding this parameter would affect them, and review the `StepRow` implementation.

**The placeholder**

A field is `user-select: text` so it can be typed in, and a placeholder sits inside that field, so a select all painted a band over the app's own words in every empty box. It is shut now while the box is empty, and it opens again on the first keystroke. A click and a keystroke both still land, checked in a real window.

Two reasons it survived the last pass. A placeholder is **painted over and never copied**, so anything that reads the selection back sees an empty string and says all is well. And the fix cannot live in the base layer with the rest: tldraw ships an unlayered `input { user-select: text }`, and a rule in no layer beats every layer whatever either side is written with, so inside the layer the fix would have worked until somebody opened a board and stopped working from then on. The panel inherits its background from the parent container, which is likely `ink-900` from `AsideView`. Since `ScrollFade` is already used consistently across similar panels like `TasksPanel` and `PlanView`, I'll keep it as-is.

Now I'm building the SubagentList component with a Row subcomponent that displays each subagent run with a mark, subject text, and loading state, then wrapping the list in ScrollFade with scroll edge detection.

I'm reconsidering the layout structure — the parent ScreenSwap with fill likely uses absolute positioning, so I need to make sure SubagentList's outer container is relative with full height, then nest the scrollable div inside to avoid layout conflicts.

Now I'm looking at how helper identity works in the thread system — ThreadItem gets an optional helperSeed field, and buildThread accepts an `as` parameter with name and seed to track which helper generated the work, so entries are attributed correctly under the helper's own identity rather than the parent agent's.

In the spoke function, I'm checking whether we're in a helper context — if so, use the helper's name and seed, otherwise use the agent's label and ID. Then I need to refactor how stepItem gets called so it receives the computed author name from spoke, which means extracting that first before building the item.

For agent.end, I'm pushing a reply object and need to be careful about the order of spread operations — spoke's author and authorId fields should come before the explicit agentId assignment to avoid unintended overwrites. Also need to check the thread.ag reference.

In the chat message rendering, I'm conditionally showing either a linked time display, a SubagentMark if there's a helperSeed, an AgentIcon if there's an agentSeed, or a regular Avatar with the author name. For SubagentRun, I'm memoizing the helper object from the thread data.

Now for the header section, I'm building the SubagentPanel header with a screen swap button that toggles between back and top views depending on whether we're inside a helper thread, along with a tooltip and button for navigating to all helpers. I'm reconsidering what "left-aligned with the back chevron" actually means. It could mean the text sits on the same row as the chevron, or it could mean the text's left edge aligns with where the chevron starts. Looking at the current layout, the chevron takes up its own row and the description is indented below it, but maybe the intent is to remove that indent so the text starts flush at the same horizontal position as the chevron. The description line could sit beside the chevron on the same row, which matches the ScreenSwap pattern and uses space efficiently. But "left-aligned with the back chevron" suggests they should share a left edge, meaning the description sits below. Maybe Jamel means the whole header row—chevron plus description—should start at the left edge, which could work either way depending on how it's interpreted. So the first layout—chevron and subject on one line with the divider below—is the stronger design choice and matches what he meant by "at the top" and "just have the line." The `max-w-full` constraint on the button is limited by its containing block—the `pl-14` div's content box, which is reduced by the padding. The `-ml-2` negative margin shifts it left by 8px, but that doesn't solve the core issue: if the button's minimum content width exceeds the available space after accounting for the padding, `max-width` won't force it to shrink below that minimum.

Looking at the actual content—`Label` with "Updated tasks" (~95px) plus the counts, totaling around 250px—that should fit comfortably within the 392px available space (480 - 56 padding - 32 margin). So the overflow isn't coming from the content itself. I keep coming back to the scroller's own `px-4` padding combined with `overflow-y-auto`. In Chromium, the scrollable overflow area for a scroll container includes the container's end-side padding added to the content's right edge, which could be pushing things beyond the visible bounds.

But wait—there's the `-ml-2` negative margin on the step row button inside the scroll container. That's the real culprit. A block child with negative left margin inside a scroller creates an interesting situation: the scrollable overflow region doesn't include content overflowing on the start side (it just clips), but with `max-w-full` on the button, its max-width is 100% of the parent's content width, and starting at -8px means it extends further than expected.

Actually, I'm overthinking this. The fix is `overflow-x-hidden` on the scroll container. But before I commit to that, let me check if there's a script in the repo to visually inspect the renderer UI and see what's actually happening.

I'm second-guessing whether I should've changed `openSubagent` to reuse the parent's tab instead of looking for an already-open tab showing that specific helper. The old behavior would find a tab with a matching threadId and bring it forward, or create a new one if needed—so opening different helpers would spawn separate tabs. But now I'm not sure if that's the right approach based on what I documented in AGENTS.md about tabs being closable and allowing multiple instances.

There's a real design tension here: `showSubagents` reuses tabs by `parentThreadId`, and the back button in the panel converts a helper tab back into the list by clearing the threadId. So the tab already operates as "one tab per parent thread, navigating between list and helper views." Under my old code, opening a second helper while one was open would create a second tab with the same parentThreadId, which `showSubagents` would then find inconsistently. My change makes this coherent—one helpers tab per thread, navigating between the list and whichever helper is active, matching the panel's two-screen design and the toggle button I'm adding. But I'm losing the ability to have several helpers open at once, and I'm not sure if that's a regression the user would actually notice or care about.

With chips in the thread, clicking helper A then helper B just replaces the view rather than opening two tabs side by side. You can't watch two at once anyway since there's only one panel. Tabs let you flip between them, but the list screen does that in one press. I think one tab per thread is simpler and makes the header toggle honest, but it does change behavior beyond what was asked. The safer approach would be to keep the "one tab per helper" behavior but record the parent so the toggle can find it—but then `closeSubagents` becomes ambiguous if there are several tabs. A toggle whose "off" state is unclear isn't simple. Maybe the button shouldn't be a toggle at all; the plan and board buttons toggle because those are pinned singular tabs, but helpers is just an ordinary tab. A simpler behavior might be to have the button just open the helpers tab rather than toggle it. I need to verify that closing tabs works correctly and that `closeSubagents` does what I expect. Then I'll update `SubagentChips` to pass the parent thread ID and add the header button. There's also an issue where `SubagentRun` doesn't pass `threadId` to `ThreadItems`, so helpers showing their own thread's chips won't have the context they need.

step.text:
The panel opens when there are tabs, so a generic open/close button in the thread header would either open it to an empty landing page or close all tabs. Jamel wants to replace the dedicated plan and other buttons with this single toggle, then let users add helpers, boards, and other items via a plus button in the panel, similar to how Codex handles an empty browser state.

I need to rethink the state model here — right now the panel only exists when tabs exist, but I should make `open` an explicit boolean flag that gets set true when any tab opens and false on closeAll, so the SidePanel can read directly from that state rather than inferring visibility from tab count.

The tricky part is handling cases like `hidePlan` where the app removes a tab as you navigate away from a thread — if that empties the tabs but you never explicitly opened the panel, it shouldn't stay open showing an empty landing page. So the rule should be: `open` becomes true when you ask for it or when a tab opens, and it becomes false when the app removes the last tab (since that's the app taking action, not you closing anything).

Actually, looking at the Codex screenshot, the panel stays open on the landing page even after the last tab closes — that's the desired behavior. So `open` should be its own independent flag: it turns true when the button is pressed or when a tab opens, and only turns false when you press the button again or click the close X. Closing the last tab leaves the panel open on the landing page, which matches what Codex shows and makes the landing page actually reachable.

But there's a problem with `hidePlan` and `hideWork` — they remove tabs automatically without user action. If one of those removes the only tab in the panel, you're left with an empty shell showing the landing rows, which feels wrong. The honest rule is: if hiding a tab leaves nothing behind, the panel should close too. I'll write that as a helper in the store so the logic lives in one place.

Now for `closeTab` when it's the last tab — that's different because you're closing it intentionally. Leaving the landing visible makes sense there, you're still in the panel but with nothing open. The X button in the header currently does `closeAll`, but with the panel having its own open state, it should just close the panel entirely. The header should always have the X button available as the way out, not just when there are tabs. Though there's also the close button in the thread header, so two exits is fine — I've seen Codex do something similar with a sidebar toggle in the top right.

Looking at the Codex approach, the panel toggle and expand icon are both there. So I should keep the X but make it close the panel, and I need to decide whether closing the panel also closes the tabs or preserves them for when you reopen. Preserving them feels better — that's the whole point of a toggle rather than a destructive close. But then the label "Close" on the X button becomes misleading.

The real tension is that if the X just closes the panel and leaves tabs intact, I lose the ability to close all tabs from the header (except via right-click menu). If the X closes everything, then I have two different meanings for "close" depending on context. Maybe the cleanest move is to drop the X entirely and put the panel toggle button in the header instead — though that duplicates the toggle that's already in the thread header. Let me check what Jamel actually asked for: just a generic open/close Browser button in that spot, removing the dedicated plan buttons.

So the scope is: the thread header gets one toggle, the plus menu conditionally shows Plan/Board/Helpers options, and there's a landing page when the panel is empty. The landing page and plus menu should read from the same list of tool kinds rather than duplicating that logic.

I'm creating a `panelOpens.ts` file that defines what the side panel can open — each option with its label, icon, conditional availability based on thread state, and what action it triggers. Both the plus menu and landing page will reference this single source of truth.

Now I need to check if Crew already has keyboard shortcuts for these actions, since the Codex design shows shortcut keys like ⌘T and ⌘P. I should only display shortcuts that actually have listeners in the codebase.

I'm also wondering where the thread header button lives in the chat view versus the thread view — it might need to live in the top bar when you're not in a thread context. Let me examine the TopBar and App.tsx to understand the layout better.

+ export const useBrowser = create<BrowserState>((write, get) => {
+   // Putting something in the panel opens it, and that is written here rather
+   // than on each of the dozen ways in, so a thirteenth cannot open a tab into a
+   // panel nobody can see. It counts what arrived rather than what is there: a
+   // page that finished loading while the panel was put away is not a way in.
+   const set: typeof write = (patch, replace) => {
+     const before = get().tabs.length
+     write(patch as never, replace as never)
+     if (get().tabs.length > before) write({ open: true } as never)
+   }
+ 
+   // A tab that takes itself away as you move takes the panel with it when it was
+   // the only thing there. The plan and the board arrive with the thread they
+   // belong to rather than by being asked for, so a panel left standing empty
+   // behind one is a panel nobody opened.
+   const settle = () => {
+     if (get().tabs.length === 0) write({ open: false } as never)

+ import { useMemo, type ReactNode } from 'react'
+ import {

+ // The one table of what the side panel can hold. The menu the plus opens and
+ // the screen an empty panel shows both read it, so the words somebody picked
+ // from are the words they are shown either way.
+ //
+ // The thread's own things stand first and come and go with the thread you are

+ // travel.

+   id: string
+   label: string
+   mark: ReactNode
+   open: () => void
+ }
+ 
+ export function usePanelOpens(): PanelOpen[] {
+   const threadId = useCrew(s => s.openThreadId)
+   const plan = useCrew(s => (s.openThreadId ? Boolean(s.threads[s.openThreadId]?.plan) : false))
+   const tickets = useCrew(s => (s.openThreadId ? Boolean(s.threads[s.openThreadId]?.tickets) : false))
+   const events = useCrew(s => s.events)
+   const helpers = useMemo(
+     () => Boolean(threadId) && events.some(e => e.kind === 'subagent.started' && e.parentThreadId === threadId),
+     [events, threadId]
+   )
+ 
+   return useMemo(() => {
+     const browser = useBrowser.getState
+     const rows: PanelOpen[] = []
+     if (threadId && plan)
+       rows.push({ id: 'plan', label: 'Plan', mark: <ChecklistGlyph />, open: () => browser().showPlan(threadId) })
+     if (threadId && tickets)
+       rows.push({ id: 'work', label: 'Board', mark: <TicketGlyph />, open: () => browser().showWork(threadId) })
+     if (threadId && helpers)
+       rows.push({
+         id: 'agent',
+         label: 'Helpers',
+         mark: <GroupGlyph />,
+         open: () => browser().showSubagents(threadId)
+       })
+     rows.push(
+       { id: 'web', label: 'Web page', mark: <GlobeGlyph />, open: () => browser().addTab() },
+       { id: 'terminal', label: 'Terminal', mark: <TerminalGlyph />, open: () => browser().addTerminal() },
+       { id: 'file', label: 'Files', mark: <FolderGlyph />, open: () => browser().openFiles() },
+       { id: 'music', label: 'Music', mark: <MusicGlyph />, open: () => browser().openMusic() },
+       { id: 'game', label: 'Games', mark: <GameGlyph />, open: () => browser().openGame() }
+     )
+     return rows
+   }, [threadId, plan, tickets, helpers])
+ }

Build a temp dir with `index.html`, a `main.tsx` that stubs `useCrew.setState({...})`
and renders the component at a fixed size, and a `probe.css`. **The css must be**

```css
@import "<repo>/src/renderer/src/styles.css";
@source "<repo>/src/renderer/src";
```

**Why:** Tailwind v4 detects content from the vite root. Importing `styles.css`
directly from a probe outside the repo compiles only the classes used in the probe
file itself, so the component renders completely unstyled and looks broken for a
reason that has nothing to do with the component. `@source` points the scan back at
the real tree.

**How to apply:** Put the probe under `node_modules/.<name>/` so nothing lands in
the auto-committing tree, `npx vite build --config <probe>/vite.config.ts`, then an
Electron main that `loadFile`s the built `dist/index.html`, waits ~1s and writes
`capturePage().toPNG()`. Delete the probe afterwards. Same shape as
`scripts/cover-sheet.mjs`, which is the committed version of this trick.

The vite config needs `base: './'`. Without it the built html asks for
`/assets/index.js`, which under `file://` is the disk root, so the page loads,
`did-finish-load` fires, nothing throws, and the capture is a black rectangle.
Check `document.getElementById('root').innerHTML.length` before believing a blank
shot. To see a `:hover` state, `webContents.insertCSS` the state on before capture,
since nothing can hover a headless window.
Related: [[crew-design-system]].

+ ## The side panel
+ 
+ Everything the app can stand beside the chat: a web page, a terminal, the project files, the music, the games, and the thread's own plan, board and helpers. `SidePanel` holds it and `BrowserPanel` draws it.

For the test cases, I need to verify the fades appear at both edges and that opacity changes based on scroll position. With scrollHeight 2000 and clientHeight 500, scrolling to the top shows the bottom fade (opacity-100) while hiding the top fade (opacity-0), and scrolling to the bottom reverses that. The useScrollEdges hook listens via addEventListener, so fireEvent.scroll works. One thing to watch: useStickToBottom's useLayoutEffect sets scrollTop to scrollHeight on mount, which means a fresh thread lands at the bottom—so the initial state should have the bottom fade hidden and the top fade visible.

I'll create the test file following the repo's naming convention and make sure the store's useCrew hook has access to the window.crew bridge that gets set up in beforeEach.

files.diff:
+ // @vitest-environment jsdom
+ import { cleanup, fireEvent, render } from '@testing-library/react'
+ import { createElement } from 'react'
+ import { afterEach, beforeEach, describe, expect, it } from 'vitest'
+ import type { ThreadMeta } from '../src/renderer/src/state/store'
+ 
+ class TestResizeObserver {
+   observe(): void {}
+   unobserve(): void {}
+   disconnect(): void {}
+ }
+ 
+ global.ResizeObserver = TestResizeObserver as unknown as typeof ResizeObserver
+ 
+ const tops = new WeakMap<HTMLElement, number>()
+ const scrollHeight = 2000
+ const clientHeight = 500
+ 
+ Object.defineProperty(HTMLElement.prototype, 'scrollHeight', { configurable: true, get: () => scrollHeight })
+ Object.defineProperty(HTMLElement.prototype, 'clientHeight', { configurable: true, get: () => clientHeight })
+ Object.defineProperty(HTMLElement.prototype, 'scrollTop', {
+   configurable: true,
+   get(this: HTMLElement) {
+     return tops.get(this) ?? 0
+   },
+   set(this: HTMLElement, value: number) {
+     tops.set(this, value)
+   }
+ })
+ 
+ const { useCrew } = await import('../src/renderer/src/state/store')
+ const SubagentRun = (await import('../src/renderer/src/components/subagents/SubagentRun')).default
+ 
+ const CHILD = 'child-thread'
+ 
+ const thread: ThreadMeta = {
+   id: CHILD,
+   agentId: 'agent-1',
+   agentLabel: 'Bubbles',
+   title: 'A helper',
+   createdBy: 'Jamel',
+   status: 'open',
+   mode: 'build',
+   parentThreadId: 'parent-thread',
+   helper: 'Scout'
+ }
+ 
+ beforeEach(() => {
+   Element.prototype.scrollIntoView = () => {}
+   window.crew = { warmTerminal: () => undefined } as unknown as CrewBridge
+   useCrew.setState({
+     threads: { [CHILD]: thread },
+     events: [],
+     steps: {},
+     threadPrompts: {},
+     threadDrafts: {},
+     queues: {},
+     tokens: {},
+     pending: {}
+   })
+ })
+ 
+ afterEach(cleanup)
+ 
+ function boot() {
+   const view = render(createElement(SubagentRun, { threadId: CHILD }))
+   const scroller = view.container.querySelector('.overflow-y-auto') as HTMLElement
+   const top = () => view.container.querySelector('.top-0.bg-gradient-to-b') as HTMLElement
+   const bottom = () => view.container.querySelector('.bottom-0.bg-gradient-to-t') as HTMLElement
+   return { scroller, top, bottom }
+ }
+ 
+ // The transcript is cut hard at both ends of the panel, under the header row and
+ // over the composer, so it goes out the way every other panel's does.
+ describe('a helper thread in the panel', () => {
+   it('fades where the words run under the chrome', () => {
+     const { scroller, top, bottom } = boot()
+ 
+     expect(top()).toBeTruthy()
+     expect(bottom()).toBeTruthy()
+ 
+     // It lands at the bottom, so what is cut off is above.
+     expect(top().className).toContain('opacity-100')
+     expect(bottom().className).toContain('opacity-0')
+ 
+     scroller.scrollTop = 0
+     fireEvent.scroll(scroller)
+ 
+     expect(top().className).toContain('opacity-0')
+     expect(bottom().className).toContain('opacity-100')
+   })
+ })
+

I'm following the same pattern as `tray-position.ts` by putting the geometry logic in its own file with tests. For the scribe spot placement, I need to decide whether it should remember where the user last positioned it, or default to the bottom center of the primary display—or maybe follow the pointer's current display instead.

The real issue is that `resize()` triggers `place()` which re-reads the cursor position, so if the mouse moves between the initial show and the ResizeObserver firing, the pill jumps to a different display. That's probably what feels random to the user—not the initial placement, but the unexpected repositioning after load.

The fix involves storing the position once it's been moved so it persists across restarts, preventing any re-placement on resize by anchoring the bottom edge and horizontal center while growing upward, clamping the remembered position to the current display's work area if the original display is gone, and making the pill draggable with the standard app-drag regions and buttons marked as no-drag. I'm considering whether to use the native `-webkit-app-region: drag` on macOS panels or implement manual pointer-drag handling for more deterministic control. NSPanel handles window dragging through Chromium's app-region implementation, which should work fine, but since I can't test this natively on a real desktop, manual drag via pointer events and `setBounds` is the safer bet—it's deterministic, lets me persist and clamp the position precisely, and I can show a grab cursor to indicate it's draggable.

For the pointer events on a non-focusable window, `pointermove` and `pointerup` will fire since non-focusable doesn't mean non-interactive (the buttons already work), and `setPointerCapture` should handle this robustly. The key insight is using screen coordinates (`screenX`/`screenY`) which are absolute and don't shift when the window moves, so I can record the initial screen point on pointerdown and send deltas to the main process to clamp and set bounds without any feedback loops.

I'm setting up a message protocol: `scribe:grab` to capture the window's starting bounds, `scribe:drag` with computed `{dx, dy}` deltas to move the window, and `scribe:drop` to save the final position. The main process applies the deltas to the captured origin and clamps the result. Now I'm working through whether to use CSS pixels or screen pixels for the delta calculations.

Since `screenX` in Chromium and Electron's DIP coordinates align when zoom is 1, I can use them directly without conversion. I'll skip the `-webkit-app-region: drag` approach since manual pointer events are cleaner and won't conflict. For the cursor, I'll use standard `cursor-grab` and `cursor-grabbing` on the pill body. I'm also writing a function to position the window at a sensible default—bottom center, slightly lifted—and clamp it to stay within bounds.

For the display selection, I'll check which screen the cursor is on when the window first appears, not during resizes. Once the user moves it, that position gets remembered. With the resize bug fixed, the default placement will be consistent, and the dragging plus persistence should solve the random positioning issue.

+ export interface Box {
+   x: number
+   y: number
+   width: number
+   height: number
+ }
+ 
+ export interface Size {
+   width: number
+   height: number
+ }
+ 
+ export interface Spot {
+   x: number
+   y: number
+ }
+ 
+ // How far off the bottom of the screen it rests before anybody has moved it.
+ // Low enough to be out of the way of what is being typed in and high enough to
+ // clear a dock.
+ const LIFT = 96
+ 
+ // It never sits hard against an edge, so a pill dragged into a corner still
+ // reads as floating over the screen rather than stuck to it.
+ const EDGE = 8
+ 
+ // Where the pill stands when nobody has put it anywhere: the bottom middle of
+ // the screen. Worked out once when it is shown rather than every time it
+ // changes height, or the pill walks across the screen while it is being read.
+ export function restSpot(work: Box, pill: Size): Spot {
+   return hold(
+     {
+       x: work.x + work.width / 2 - pill.width / 2,
+       y: work.y + work.height - pill.height - LIFT
+     },
+     pill,
+     work
+   )
+ }
+ 
+ // A spot is only ever as good as the screen it was written down on. A monitor
+ // that has been unplugged since, or one that changed resolution, would leave
+ // the pill somewhere nobody can see it, so every spot is held inside the work
+ // area it is going to be drawn in.
+ export function hold(spot: Spot, pill: Size, work: Box): Spot {
+   const right = work.x + work.width - pill.width - EDGE
+   const bottom = work.y + work.height - pill.height - EDGE
+   return {
+     x: Math.round(Math.max(work.x + EDGE, Math.min(spot.x, right))),
+     y: Math.round(Math.max(work.y + EDGE, Math.min(spot.y, bottom)))
+   }
+ }
+ 
+ // Growing keeps the bottom edge where it is, so the two buttons stay under the
+ // pointer that is reaching for them. Anchored at the top instead, a pill that
+ // grows a line pushes its own check button down and out from under the finger
+ // already on the way to it.
+ export function grown(box: Box, height: number, work: Box): Spot {
+   return hold(
+     { x: box.x, y: box.y + box.height - height },
+     { width: box.width, height },
+     work
+   )
+ }
+ 
+ // The point a box is judged by when it is being dragged between screens: the
+ // middle of it, so the pill lands on the screen it is mostly over rather than
+ // on whichever one its top left corner happens to have crossed into.
+ export function middle(box: Box): Spot {
+   return { x: Math.round(box.x + box.width / 2), y: Math.round(box.y + box.height / 2) }
+ }
+ 
+ // What was written down last time, if it is a pair of real numbers. Anything
+ // else is a machine that has never moved the pill, which is the rest spot.
+ export function spotFrom(value: unknown): Spot | null {
+   const saved = value as Partial<Spot> | null
+   if (!saved || !Number.isFinite(saved.x) || !Number.isFinite(saved.y)) return null
+   return { x: Math.round(saved.x as number), y: Math.round(saved.y as number) }
+ }
+

+ import fs from 'node:fs'
+ import { BrowserWindow, screen } from 'electron'
+ import type { ScribeSettings } from '../shared/scribe'
+ import { grown, hold, middle, restSpot, spotFrom, type Spot } from './scribe-spot'
+ import type { PanelPage } from './tray-panel'
+ import { createScribeOptions } from './window-options'
+ 
+ // The pill, and the window it stands in. Frameless, transparent, above
+ // everything, and never focused: whatever you were typing in has to keep the
+ // caret, or a dictation would land nowhere.
+ 
+ const WIDTH = 216
+ const HEIGHT = 56
+ const MAX_HEIGHT = 140
+ 
+ export class ScribeWindow {
+   private win: BrowserWindow | null = null
+   private settings: ScribeSettings | null = null
+   private file: string | null = null
+   // Where it was put, which is a decision somebody made once and should not
+   // have to make again. Null until they make it, and the bottom middle of the
+   // screen until then.
+   private spot: Spot | null = null
+   // Where the pill stood when it was taken hold of. Every move is measured
+   // from here rather than from where it has got to, so a drag that runs into
+   // the edge of a screen comes back off it as the pointer does.
+   private held: Spot | null = null
+ 
+   constructor(private readonly page: PanelPage) {}
+ 
+   owns(win: BrowserWindow): boolean {
+     return this.win === win
+   }
+ 
+   // Built and loaded before anyone presses the key, the way the tray panel is,
+   // and for a bigger reason: this window holds whisper, and a model that has to
+   // be fetched at the moment somebody starts talking is a first dictation that
+   // arrives a minute late.
+   warm(): void {
+     this.window()
+   }
+ 
+   remember(file: string): void {
+     this.file = file
+     try {
+       this.spot = spotFrom(JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(file, 'utf8')))
+     } catch {
+       this.spot = null
+     }
+   }
+ 
+   show(): void {
+     const win = this.window()
+     this.place()
+     // Never `show`, which would take the focus off the app being dictated into
+     // and land the paste in the wrong place, or nowhere at all.
+     win.showInactive()
+   }
+ 
+   hide(): void {
+     this.win?.hide()
+   }
+ 
+   get showing(): boolean {
+     return this.win?.isVisible() ?? false
+   }
+ 
+   send(channel: string, ...args: unknown[]): void {
+     const win = this.win
+     if (!win || win.webContents.isDestroyed()) return
+     win.webContents.send(channel, ...args)
+   }
+ 
+   apply(settings: ScribeSettings): void {
+     this.settings = settings
+     this.send('scribe:settings', settings)
+   }
+ 
+   // A pill that has grown a line keeps its bottom edge and its left edge. It is
+   // never placed again after it is shown: placing reads the pointer, and the
+   // pointer has moved on by the time the renderer has measured itself, which is
+   // what made the pill land somewhere different every time.
+   resize(height: number): void {
+     const win = this.win
+     if (!win) return
+     const wanted = Math.round(Math.max(HEIGHT, Math.min(height, MAX_HEIGHT)))
+     const box = win.getBounds()
+     if (box.height === wanted) return
+     const spot = grown(box, wanted, this.workNear(middle({ ...box, height: wanted })))
+     win.setBounds({ ...spot, width: box.width, height: wanted })
+     this.spot = spot
+   }
+ 
+   grab(): void {
+     this.held = this.win ? { x: this.win.getBounds().x, y: this.win.getBounds().y } : null
+   }
+ 
+   // Dragged by however far the pointer has travelled since it took hold, and
+   // held inside whichever screen the pill is now mostly over, so it can be
+   // moved to another monitor and cannot be pushed off the edge of one.
+   drag(by: Spot, settled: boolean): void {
+     const win = this.win
+     const from = this.held
+     if (!win || !from) return
+     const box = win.getBounds()
+     const wanted = { x: from.x + by.x, y: from.y + by.y }
+     const spot = hold(wanted, box, this.workNear(middle({ ...box, ...wanted })))
+     win.setBounds({ ...box, ...spot })
+     this.spot = spot
+     if (!settled) return
+     this.held = null
+     this.write(spot)
+   }
+ 
+   close(): void {
+     this.win?.destroy()
+     this.win = null
+   }
+ 
+   private write(spot: Spot): void {
+     if (!this.file) return
+     try {
+       fs.writeFileSync(this.file, JSON.stringify(spot))
+     } catch {}
+   }
+ 
+   private workNear(point: Spot): Electron.Rectangle {
+     return screen.getDisplayNearestPoint(point).workArea
+   }
+ 
+   // Where it was left, if it was ever moved. Otherwise the bottom middle of the
+   // screen the pointer is on, which is the screen the app being typed into is
+   // almost certainly on.
+   private place(): void {
+     const win = this.win
+     if (!win) return
+     const box = win.getBounds()
+     const spot = this.spot
+       ? hold(this.spot, box, this.workNear(middle({ ...box, ...this.spot })))
+       : restSpot(this.workNear(screen.getCursorScreenPoint()), box)
+     win.setBounds({ ...box, ...spot })
+   }
+ 
+   private window(): BrowserWindow {
+     if (this.win) return this.win
+     const win = new BrowserWindow(
+       createScribeOptions(process.platform, this.page.preload, { width: WIDTH, height: HEIGHT })
+     )
+     // Above a full screen app and on whichever space is in front. Never this
+     // call without `skipTransformProcessType`: it turns the app into an
+     // accessory on macOS and the icon leaves the dock for good.
+     win.setAlwaysOnTop(true, 'screen-saver')
+     win.setVisibleOnAllWorkspaces(true, {
+       visibleOnFullScreen: true,
+       skipTransformProcessType: true
+     })
+     win.excludedFromShownWindowsMenu = true
+     win.on('closed', () => {
+       this.win = null
+     })
+     win.webContents.once('did-finish-load', () => {
+       if (this.settings) win.webContents.send('scribe:settings', this.settings)
+     })
+     if (this.page.devUrl) void win.loadURL(`${this.page.devUrl}#scribe`)
+     else void win.loadFile(this.page.file, { hash: 'scribe' })
+     this.win = win
+     return win
+   }
+ }

+ import type { PointerEvent as Pressed } from 'react'
+ 
+ // Taking hold of the pill and putting it somewhere else. The window is what
+ // moves, so a drag is a distance handed to main rather than anything this page
+ // does to itself.
+ //
+ // It is measured against the screen and never against the window, because the
+ // window travels under the pointer the whole time it is being dragged. Read the
+ // other way round, every frame would move the pill by however far it had
+ // already moved, and it would run off the edge of the screen on its own.
+ export function grab(event: Pressed<HTMLElement>): void {
+   if (event.button !== 0) return
+   const box = event.currentTarget
+   const from = { x: event.screenX, y: event.screenY }
+   window.crew.grabScribe()
+   box.setPointerCapture(event.pointerId)
+ 
+   const move = (moved: PointerEvent) =>
+     window.crew.moveScribe(moved.screenX - from.x, moved.screenY - from.y, false)
+ 
+   // A drag that is let go of and one the system takes away both settle where
+   // the pill stands, so a gesture interrupted by anything at all still leaves
+   // it somewhere it will be found again.
+   const settle = (last: PointerEvent) => {
+     window.crew.moveScribe(last.screenX - from.x, last.screenY - from.y, true)
+     box.removeEventListener('pointermove', move)
+     box.removeEventListener('pointerup', settle)
+     box.removeEventListener('pointercancel', settle)
+   }
+ 
+   box.addEventListener('pointermove', move)
+   box.addEventListener('pointerup', settle)
+   box.addEventListener('pointercancel', settle)
+ }
+

## Why it looked random

It was placed at the bottom middle of the screen **your pointer was on**, and then placed *again* every time the renderer measured itself. Those are two different moments, and your pointer has moved between them, so a pill shown on one screen could land on another a frame later. It goes between monitors, and it is held inside whichever screen it is mostly over. A spot left on a monitor you have since unplugged comes back onto one that is really there rather than opening somewhere you cannot see.
